new_words.english_meaning: Having a sharp, pungent taste that is not sweet, like black coffee or dark chocolate.
new_words.gujarati_meaning: કડવો સ્વાદ — જેમ કે કાળી કૉફી અથવા ડાર્ક ચૉકલેટ જેવો તીખો, અળખામણો સ્વાદ.
new_words.usage_note: Used to describe a taste that many find unpleasant, though some foods like dark chocolate are valued for their bitterness.
new_words.memory_tip: 'bitter' = કડવું → bitter taste = કડવો સ્વાદ, જેવો કે કારેલાનો.
examples: The medicine had a bitter taste that was hard to swallow.
She prefers bitter dark chocolate over sweet milk chocolate.
The bitter flavour of the coffee woke him up instantly.
Bitter melon is commonly used in South Asian cooking.

new_words.english_meaning: Having an acidic taste like lemon juice or vinegar; not sweet.
new_words.gujarati_meaning: ખાટો સ્વાદ — જેવો કે લીંબુ અથવા વિનેગરનો, ન મીઠો.
new_words.usage_note: Sour is a basic taste descriptor. 'Turn sour' can also mean food has spoiled.
examples: The yogurt had a pleasantly sour taste.
She made a sour face after biting into the unripe mango.
Sour cream is used as a topping for baked potatoes.
The milk turned sour after being left out overnight.

new_words.english_meaning: Having the pleasant taste characteristic of sugar or honey.
new_words.gujarati_meaning: મીઠો સ્વાદ — ખાંડ અથવા મધ જેવો આહ્લાદક સ્વાદ.
new_words.usage_note: A 'sweet tooth' means a person who loves sweet foods. 'Bittersweet' describes something both good and sad.
examples: The ripe mango was incredibly sweet.
She has a sweet tooth and loves desserts.
The sauce had a sweet and sour balance.
This tea is too sweet for my taste.

new_words.english_meaning: Having a strong, hot flavour from spices such as chilli or pepper.
new_words.gujarati_meaning: મસાલેદાર અથવા તીખો — મરચા અથવા મરી જેવા મસાલાઓથી આવતો ઉગ્ર સ્વાદ.
new_words.usage_note: Spicy usually refers to heat from chilli. Do not confuse with 'spiced', which simply means seasoned with spices.
examples: He loves spicy food and always orders the hottest dish.
The curry was so spicy it made her eyes water.
Indian cuisine is known for its spicy flavours.
Add less chilli if you don't want it too spicy.

new_words.english_meaning: Having a flavour that resembles or is produced by smoke, often from grilling or barbecuing.
new_words.gujarati_meaning: ધૂમ્ +'ઓ જેવો સ્વાદ — ગ્રિલ અથવા બાર્બેક્યૂ કરવાથી આવતો ધ'ઓ-ભ'ર'ઓ સ'ડ'.
new_words.usage_note: Smoky paprika (smoked paprika) is a popular way to add smoky flavour without a grill. Smoky flavour is central to barbecue cuisine.
examples: The barbecued ribs had a wonderful smoky flavour.
She added smoked paprika for a smoky depth.
The cheese had a rich, smoky taste.
Smoky lentil soup is a winter favourite.

new_words.english_meaning: A savoury, meaty taste considered the fifth basic taste, found in foods like mushrooms, soy sauce, and aged cheese.
new_words.gujarati_meaning: પાંચમો મૂળ સ્વાદ — ઘૂંટાઈ ગયેલ, ભારે અને ભૂ' ,'ગ'ડ' એ'વ' સ'ડ', જ' ,'ઉ, ,'ઓ'ય ,'ઓ'સ, ,'ગ' ,'ઝ'.
new_words.usage_note: Umami is a Japanese word and concept, now widely used in English culinary contexts.
examples: Mushrooms add an umami depth to the soup.
Soy sauce is a great source of umami.
Chefs often use parmesan rind to add umami to sauces.
The umami flavour in the broth made it incredibly satisfying.

new_words.english_meaning: Having a sharply strong taste or smell that is often overpowering.
new_words.usage_note: Pungent describes both taste and smell. Often used for garlic, onions, or strong cheeses.
examples: The pungent smell of garlic filled the kitchen.
Blue cheese has a very pungent flavour.
Some people dislike the pungent taste of durian.
The pungent curry made everyone's eyes water.

new_words.english_meaning: Having a soft, smooth, and rich flavour without sharpness or bitterness.
new_words.usage_note: Mellow is often used for aged wines, cheeses, or coffees that have developed a smooth, rich character over time.
examples: The aged cheddar had a mellow, nutty flavour.
This wine is very mellow and easy to drink.
Roasting garlic makes it mellow and sweet.
The coffee had a mellow taste with hints of chocolate.

new_words.english_meaning: Having a sharp, acidic flavour; pleasantly sour.
new_words.usage_note: Tart implies a sharper, more refreshing sourness than simply 'sour'. Also a noun for a pastry with an open top.
examples: The cranberries were wonderfully tart.
She liked the tart flavour of the lemon tart.
Rhubarb has a naturally tart taste.
The dressing was tart but balanced with a little honey.

new_words.english_meaning: Lacking flavour or taste; dull and uninteresting to eat.
new_words.usage_note: Insipid is a formal, slightly literary word. In everyday speech, 'bland' or 'tasteless' are more common.
examples: The soup was watery and insipid.
She found the hospital food insipid and unappetising.
Without seasoning, the dish was completely insipid.
He complained that the boiled vegetables were insipid.

new_words.english_meaning: To briefly plunge food into boiling water and then into cold water to stop cooking, in order to soften or preserve colour.
new_words.usage_note: Blanching is a common prep technique before freezing vegetables to preserve their colour and texture.
examples: Blanch the broccoli for two minutes before adding it to the stir-fry.
She blanched the almonds to remove their skins easily.
Blanching spinach before freezing helps retain its bright green colour.
You should blanch the tomatoes before peeling them.

new_words.english_meaning: To cook food slowly in a small amount of liquid in a covered pot.
new_words.usage_note: Braising is ideal for tough cuts of meat as the slow cooking breaks down the fibres, making the meat tender.
examples: She braised the lamb shanks for three hours until tender.
Braising is the best method for tough cuts of beef.
He braised the cabbage with bacon and apple.
The slow-braised pork was falling off the bone.

new_words.english_meaning: To cut food into small, uniform cube-shaped pieces.
new_words.usage_note: Dicing is more precise than chopping — the pieces are uniform cubes. 'Finely diced' means very small cubes.
examples: Dice the onions before adding them to the pan.
She finely diced the carrots for the salad.
Diced tomatoes are used as a base for many sauces.
He diced the chicken into even pieces for the curry.

new_words.english_meaning: To gently mix a light ingredient into a heavier one using a soft cutting and turning motion to preserve air.
new_words.usage_note: Folding is used in baking to keep a mixture light and airy. Overmixing deflates the batter.
examples: Fold the egg whites gently into the batter.
She carefully folded the cream into the mousse.
Fold the flour in slowly to avoid lumps.
Over-folding the mixture will make the cake dense.

new_words.english_meaning: To cut food, especially meat or garlic, into very tiny pieces.
new_words.usage_note: Minced meat (or mince) is a common ingredient in dishes like bolognese or keema.
examples: Mince the garlic finely before adding it to the oil.
She used minced beef to make the bolognese sauce.
The recipe calls for a cup of minced onion.
He minced the herbs and mixed them into the butter.

new_words.english_meaning: To cook food gently in simmering liquid, such as water, milk, or stock.
new_words.usage_note: Poaching is a gentle, healthy cooking method that keeps food moist. Poached eggs are a brunch favourite.
examples: She poached the eggs perfectly for breakfast.
Poach the salmon in white wine for extra flavour.
Poaching is a healthy way to cook chicken.
He poached the pears in spiced red wine.

new_words.english_meaning: To boil a liquid so that it evaporates and becomes thicker and more concentrated in flavour.
new_words.usage_note: Reduction is a key technique in sauce-making. 'Reduce by half' means boil until only half the liquid remains.
examples: Reduce the sauce on a low heat until it thickens.
The recipe says to reduce the stock by half.
Reducing the wine before adding cream gives a rich flavour.
She reduced the balsamic vinegar into a glossy glaze.

new_words.english_meaning: To cook food by placing it over boiling water so that the steam cooks it without contact with the water.
new_words.usage_note: Steaming retains more nutrients than boiling. Dim sum dumplings are a famous example of steamed food.
examples: Steam the broccoli for five minutes to keep it crisp.
Steamed fish is healthier than fried fish.
She steamed the dumplings in a bamboo basket.
Steam the rice instead of boiling it for fluffier results.

new_words.english_meaning: To heat sugar or foods containing sugar until they turn golden-brown and develop a rich, sweet flavour.
new_words.usage_note: Caramelised onions take 30-45 minutes on low heat. The process requires patience to develop deep, sweet flavour.
examples: Caramelise the onions slowly for the best flavour.
He caramelised the sugar to make a toffee sauce.
Caramelised bananas are delicious over ice cream.
The caramelisation of the sugar gives creme brulee its crunchy top.

new_words.english_meaning: To melt fat from meat by cooking it slowly, so the fat runs out and the meat becomes crispy.
new_words.usage_note: Rendering is commonly used for bacon, duck, or pork belly. The rendered fat can be used for frying.
examples: Render the bacon in a cold pan for the crispiest result.
Slowly render the duck fat before roasting.
Rendered lard was traditionally used for pastry.
The pork skin becomes crispy as the fat renders out.

new_words.english_meaning: A meal cooked and bought at a restaurant but eaten somewhere else, or the shop that sells such food.
new_words.usage_note: British English uses 'takeaway'; American English uses 'takeout'. Both mean the same thing.
examples: Let's order a takeaway tonight instead of cooking.
They got a Chinese takeaway and watched a film.
Takeaway food has become very popular since food delivery apps launched.
She picked up a takeaway on her way home from work.

new_words.english_meaning: A list of food and drink items available at a restaurant.
new_words.usage_note: A 'set menu' is a fixed selection of dishes at a fixed price. An 'a la carte' menu allows ordering individual items.
examples: Could we see the menu, please?
The set menu includes three courses for a fixed price.
The children's menu has simpler options.
The seasonal menu changes every three months.

new_words.english_meaning: A person who serves food and drinks to customers in a restaurant.
new_words.usage_note: Waiter (male) and waitress (female) are traditional terms. 'Server' is now commonly used for any gender.
examples: The waiter took our order promptly.
Excuse me, waiter — could we have the bill?
The waiter recommended the chef's special.
She worked as a waitress during her university days.

new_words.english_meaning: Given free of charge, especially as a gesture of goodwill in a restaurant.
new_words.usage_note: 'On the house' and 'complimentary' are synonymous in restaurant contexts. Do not confuse with 'complementary' (goes well with).
examples: The restaurant offered complimentary bread while we waited.
We received a complimentary dessert on our anniversary.
The manager sent over a complimentary bottle of wine.
Complimentary tea is available in the lounge.

new_words.english_meaning: A charge made by a restaurant for serving wine that a customer has brought themselves.
new_words.usage_note: Some restaurants are 'BYO (bring your own)' restaurants where corkage applies. Always ask about the corkage fee in advance.
examples: The restaurant charges a corkage fee of 10 pounds per bottle.
We brought our own champagne and paid the corkage.
Ask if there is a corkage charge before bringing your own wine.
Some restaurants offer no corkage on certain nights.

new_words.english_meaning: To eat a main meal, especially in a formal or restaurant setting.
new_words.usage_note: 'Dine out' means to eat at a restaurant. 'Wine and dine' means to treat someone to a good meal and drinks.
examples: They dined at an Italian restaurant to celebrate.
We dine out at least once a week.
He wined and dined his clients at a luxury restaurant.
The hotel offers a dining experience with panoramic views.

new_words.english_meaning: The first course of a meal, served before the main dish.
new_words.usage_note: In British English, 'starter' is common; in American English, 'appetizer' or 'entree' is used for the first course.
examples: I'll have the soup as a starter, please.
The starter was a beautiful smoked salmon dish.
They shared a few starters before the main course.
The restaurant is known for its inventive starters.

new_words.english_meaning: A sweet course eaten at the end of a meal.
new_words.usage_note: In British English, 'pudding' or 'afters' are informal terms for dessert. Do not confuse 'dessert' (sweet dish) with 'desert' (dry land).
examples: Would you like to see the dessert menu?
She ordered a chocolate fondant for dessert.
He was too full for dessert after the large main course.
The desserts at this bakery are legendary.

new_words.english_meaning: One of the successive parts of a meal, such as starter, main, and dessert.
new_words.usage_note: A 'three-course meal' has a starter, main, and dessert. A 'tasting menu' may have seven or more courses.
examples: We had a three-course meal for our anniversary.
The first course was a delicate mushroom soup.
A five-course tasting menu is available on weekends.
They opted for the two-course lunch deal.

new_words.english_meaning: A bag provided by a restaurant to take home leftover food from a meal.
collocations: take home in a doggy bag
new_words.usage_note: The term originally referred to telling staff the food was for a pet. Now widely accepted in most countries.
examples: Could we have a doggy bag for the leftovers?
She took the rest of her pasta home in a doggy bag.
Asking for a doggy bag helps reduce food waste.
More restaurants now offer doggy bags as standard.

new_words.english_meaning: A unit of energy provided by food, used to measure the energy content of what we eat.
new_words.usage_note: Technically, food labels show 'kilocalories' (kcal), but these are commonly called 'calories' in everyday speech.
examples: An apple contains about 80 calories.
She tracks her calorie intake every day.
Exercise helps you burn calories.
A high-calorie diet can lead to weight gain.

new_words.english_meaning: A nutrient essential for building and repairing body tissues, found in meat, eggs, beans, and dairy.
new_words.usage_note: Protein is one of three macronutrients alongside carbohydrates and fats. Athletes often increase protein intake.
examples: Chicken breast is an excellent source of lean protein.
Vegetarians can get protein from lentils and tofu.
He increased his protein intake to build muscle.
Eggs are one of the most complete protein foods.

new_words.english_meaning: A substance in plant foods that the body cannot digest, which helps keep the digestive system healthy.
new_words.usage_note: Both spellings are correct: 'fibre' (British) and 'fiber' (American). A high-fibre diet is linked to a lower risk of bowel cancer.
examples: Wholemeal bread is high in dietary fibre.
A diet rich in fibre can reduce cholesterol.
Fruits and vegetables are excellent sources of fibre.
He increased his fibre intake to improve digestion.

new_words.english_meaning: A period of time during which a person avoids unhealthy food and drink to cleanse the body.
new_words.usage_note: The scientific evidence for 'detox diets' is limited. Nutritionists note the liver and kidneys naturally detoxify the body.
examples: She went on a detox after the holiday season.
He tried a week-long juice detox.
A detox diet typically involves avoiding alcohol, caffeine, and processed foods.
Many nutritionists are sceptical about commercial detox products.

new_words.english_meaning: Describing food that contains no gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye, suitable for people with coeliac disease.
new_words.usage_note: Coeliac disease requires a strict gluten-free diet. Many people also choose gluten-free diets by preference, though this is not medically necessary.
examples: She follows a gluten-free diet due to coeliac disease.
The restaurant has a separate gluten-free menu.
Many supermarkets now stock a wide range of gluten-free products.
Gluten-free pasta is made from rice or maize flour.

new_words.english_meaning: A person who does not eat or use any animal products, including meat, dairy, and eggs.
new_words.usage_note: Veganism extends beyond diet to exclude animal products in clothing and cosmetics. Do not confuse with vegetarian, who may eat dairy and eggs.
examples: She became a vegan for environmental reasons.
Most restaurants now offer vegan options.
A vegan diet excludes all animal products.
He switched to a vegan lifestyle last year.

new_words.english_meaning: The chemical processes in the body that convert food into energy.
new_words.usage_note: A 'fast metabolism' means the body burns calories quickly. Exercise and certain foods are said to boost metabolism.
examples: Exercise can help boost your metabolism.
Her fast metabolism means she can eat a lot without gaining weight.
Thyroid problems can slow down your metabolism.
Green tea is believed to slightly increase metabolic rate.

new_words.english_meaning: A negative physical reaction to a particular food, such as difficulty digesting it, without an immune response.
new_words.usage_note: Food intolerance differs from a food allergy. Allergy involves the immune system; intolerance usually involves digestion.
examples: She has lactose intolerance and avoids dairy.
A food intolerance test can identify problem foods.
Lactose intolerance is very common in South Asian populations.
He discovered his intolerance to gluten after years of stomach problems.

new_words.english_meaning: A product taken to add vitamins, minerals, or other nutrients to the diet that may be missing.
new_words.usage_note: A supplement should complement, not replace, a healthy diet. Always consult a doctor before starting supplements.
examples: She takes a vitamin D supplement in winter.
Protein supplements are popular among gym-goers.
A balanced diet reduces the need for dietary supplements.
He supplements his diet with omega-3 fish oil capsules.

new_words.english_meaning: The process of maintaining adequate water levels in the body, essential for health.
new_words.usage_note: The body loses water through sweat, breathing, and urination. Adults are advised to drink about 2 litres of water a day.
examples: Proper hydration is essential during exercise.
He was suffering from dehydration after running the marathon.
Fruits and vegetables also contribute to daily hydration.
She carries a water bottle everywhere to stay hydrated.

new_words.english_meaning: Extremely hungry; feeling an intense desire to eat.
new_words.usage_note: Ravenous is stronger than 'hungry' or 'peckish'. It suggests an almost desperate need to eat.
examples: I am absolutely ravenous — I haven't eaten since breakfast.
The children came home from school ravenous.
After the hike, they were ravenous and ate everything in sight.
She had a ravenous appetite after being unwell for a week.

new_words.english_meaning: Completely satisfied after eating, with no desire to eat more.
new_words.usage_note: Satiated implies deep satisfaction beyond simply being 'full'. It is more formal than 'full up'.
examples: After the three-course meal, she was completely satiated.
High-protein foods keep you satiated for longer.
He felt satiated and content after the feast.
Fibre-rich foods help you feel satiated and prevent overeating.

new_words.english_meaning: To eat small amounts of food throughout the day rather than having set meals.
new_words.usage_note: Grazing can be a healthy eating pattern for some but may lead to overeating if snacks are high in calories.
examples: She tends to graze on snacks all day rather than eat proper meals.
Grazing on fruit and nuts is a healthy habit.
He grazed on leftovers while watching television.
Some nutritionists recommend grazing over three big meals.

new_words.english_meaning: Sharp, uncomfortable feelings of pain in the stomach caused by hunger.
new_words.usage_note: Hunger pangs occur when the stomach contracts in search of food. They typically last about 30 minutes.
examples: She felt hunger pangs by mid-morning as she had skipped breakfast.
Drink water to temporarily ease hunger pangs.
He ignored his hunger pangs and worked through lunch.
Hunger pangs woke him up in the middle of the night.

new_words.english_meaning: To eat a large amount of food greedily and to excess.
new_words.usage_note: Gorge implies eating well beyond what is needed. Often used reflexively: 'gorge oneself on something'.
examples: They gorged themselves on pizza after the football match.
She gorged on sweets during the festival.
It's tempting to gorge on buffet food, but try to pace yourself.
He gorged on holiday food and felt unwell afterwards.

new_words.english_meaning: To stimulate someone's appetite or desire for food.
new_words.usage_note: Used almost exclusively in the phrase 'whet the appetite'. Do not confuse with 'wet'.
examples: The smell of freshly baked bread whetted her appetite.
The teaser video whetted viewers' appetites for the new show.
A starter is meant to whet your appetite, not fill you up.
The aroma of spices whetted his appetite as he walked past the restaurant.

new_words.english_meaning: A small amount of food eaten between main meals.
new_words.usage_note: Snacking between meals can help maintain energy levels. Healthy snacks include fruit, nuts, and yoghurt.
examples: She keeps healthy snacks at her desk to avoid vending machine food.
He snacked on almonds between meetings.
Children often need an afternoon snack after school.
Late-night snacking can disrupt sleep and digestion.

new_words.english_meaning: To allow oneself to enjoy something pleasurable, especially food, beyond what is usual or advisable.
new_words.usage_note: Indulge implies pleasure with a slight sense of guilt or going beyond normal limits. 'Occasional indulgence' is a common phrase.
examples: She indulged in a large slice of chocolate cake.
It's fine to indulge occasionally as part of a balanced diet.
He indulged his sweet tooth with a box of chocolates.
Everyone deserves to indulge in their favourite food sometimes.

new_words.english_meaning: To deliberately choose not to eat or drink something, often for health or moral reasons.
new_words.usage_note: Abstain often implies willpower and self-discipline. 'Abstinence' refers to the state of abstaining.
examples: She abstained from alcohol during her pregnancy.
He abstained from meat during the religious festival.
Abstaining from sugar for a month helped him lose weight.
Many people abstain from eating after 8 pm to improve digestion.

new_words.english_meaning: To eat a very large amount of food in a short time, usually beyond what is comfortable.
new_words.usage_note: Binge eating can be a sign of an eating disorder. 'Binge-eating disorder' is a recognised medical condition requiring professional support.
examples: She binged on crisps and chocolate while watching films.
Binge eating followed by guilt is a warning sign.
He tends to binge at weekends after being strict all week.
Binge eating disorder affects millions of people worldwide.

new_words.english_meaning: Splendid and expensive-looking; describing a meal that is rich, lavish, and impressive.
new_words.usage_note: Sumptuous emphasises luxury and abundance. Often used for formal dinners or special occasions.
examples: The wedding feast was absolutely sumptuous.
They enjoyed a sumptuous three-course dinner at the hotel.
The table was laid with a sumptuous spread of dishes.
A sumptuous banquet was held in honour of the visiting dignitaries.

new_words.english_meaning: Stimulating one's appetite; looking or smelling attractive and making you want to eat.
new_words.usage_note: Appetising can describe appearance and smell. Its antonym, 'unappetising', is equally useful.
examples: The golden-brown chicken looked incredibly appetising.
The appetising aroma of garlic butter filled the room.
Colourful dishes always look more appetising.
She arranged the fruit to make the platter look appetising.

new_words.english_meaning: Lacking strong flavour, taste, or interest; mild and unexciting.
new_words.usage_note: Bland is not always negative — bland foods (rice, toast, banana) are recommended when someone is unwell.
examples: Hospital food is often criticised for being bland.
The soup was bland and needed more seasoning.
A bland diet is recommended after a stomach illness.
She found the salad bland without any dressing.

new_words.english_meaning: Good for health and well-being; describing food that is healthy, natural, and nourishing.
new_words.usage_note: Wholesome implies both physical and moral goodness — it often carries a warm, comforting connotation.
examples: She prepared a wholesome meal of grilled fish and vegetables.
The children enjoyed wholesome homemade soup.
Wholesome ingredients make for better cooking.
A wholesome breakfast sets you up for the day.

new_words.english_meaning: Rich, satisfying, and rather excessive — describing food that is pleasurable and possibly unhealthy.
new_words.usage_note: Indulgent has a positive, pleasurable connotation even though it implies something a little excessive or unhealthy.
examples: The chocolate lava cake was wonderfully indulgent.
She treated herself to an indulgent spa lunch.
It's fine to enjoy an indulgent meal occasionally.
He ordered the most indulgent item on the menu — triple chocolate brownie.

new_words.english_meaning: Extremely tasty and delicious; informally used to describe food that is wonderful to eat.
new_words.usage_note: Scrumptious is informal and enthusiastic. It is typically used in spoken English to express great pleasure at food.
examples: The homemade pie was absolutely scrumptious.
Everything at that bakery is scrumptious.
She made a scrumptious lasagne for the dinner party.
This is the most scrumptious chocolate cake I have ever tasted.

new_words.english_meaning: Having a pleasant and distinctive flavour; full of taste.
new_words.usage_note: Both 'flavoursome' (British) and 'flavorful' (American) mean the same thing. 'Flavoursome' is less common but found in British recipe writing.
examples: The slow-cooked lamb was incredibly flavoursome.
Fresh herbs make any dish more flavoursome.
The sauce was rich and flavoursome.
She used high-quality ingredients to create a flavoursome meal.

new_words.english_meaning: Cooked for too long, making the food dry, tough, or less flavourful.
new_words.usage_note: Overcooked meat becomes dry and tough; overcooked vegetables lose their nutrients and colour.
examples: The steak was unfortunately overcooked and quite tough.
Overcooked pasta loses its texture and becomes mushy.
She returned the overcooked chicken to the kitchen.
Overcooked vegetables lose most of their vitamins.

new_words.english_meaning: Not cooked enough; still raw in the centre or lacking enough heat to be safe or pleasant to eat.
new_words.usage_note: Undercooked poultry and eggs can pose serious food safety risks due to bacteria like Salmonella.
examples: The chicken was undercooked in the middle — dangerous to eat.
She sent back the undercooked rice.
Undercooked eggs can carry a risk of Salmonella.
The restaurant apologised for serving undercooked fish.

new_words.english_meaning: Decorated or embellished with a small amount of food, such as herbs, lemon, or sauce, to enhance its appearance.
new_words.usage_note: A garnish should complement the dish's flavour, not just its appearance. Common garnishes include parsley, lemon wedges, and chilli flakes.
examples: The soup was garnished with a swirl of cream and fresh chives.
Each plate was beautifully garnished with a slice of lemon.
She garnished the curry with fresh coriander leaves.
A well-garnished dish signals care and attention from the chef.
